units.sentence: If you're a student at a Georgia public high school: By Dec 31, 2026, you can't access phones or similar devices during the school day, with some exceptions.

units.sentence: Access is allowed only if a parent signs a permission form.
units.problem: Invented exception. No passage mentions a parent permission form. The law allows access only when a student's IEP, Section 504 Plan or medical plan 'explicitly mandates the use of a personal electronic device' (P-013), or when access is 'required by law' (P-007). It also contradicts lines 21, 79 and 120.
units.suggested_fix: Access is allowed only when your IEP, Section 504 plan or medical plan explicitly requires the device, or when another law requires it. [P-013, P-007]

units.sentence: If you work at a Georgia public high school: By July 1, 2027, your school must enforce the phone ban, which must include hiring a full-time phone monitor.

It says nothing about hiring or a full-time monitor. Only the first clause (schools must enforce) is supported. Line 201 states the rule correctly.
units.suggested_fix: By July 1, 2027, your school must monitor and enforce the phone ban, which may include assigning staff to oversee it. [P-007, P-014]

framing_issues.text: and Option B serves most families best
framing_issues.issue: The page recommends an option. The nonpartisan rules bar endorsements of bills or options, and no source supports it. Delete the clause.

framing_issues.text: Access is allowed only if a parent signs a permission form.
framing_issues.issue: The invented parental opt-out misleads families about how the ban works. It also undercuts the 'parental choice' argument (card 6, the Emory reasons) by implying parents already have that choice.

framing_issues.text: the law sets aside $5 million for it
framing_issues.issue: The invented appropriation makes the law look funded and softens the cost concerns in Option B's 'Who pays' and card 5. Lines 16, 29, 120 and 201 say the opposite.

framing_issues.text: If you care most about reaching your child in an emergency: ... was "Should be parental choice."
framing_issues.issue: The values guide pairs an emergency heading with the parental-choice reason and calls it the top reason. The real top reason, 'No way to reach child during emergency' (74.8%), matches the heading. As written, the line understates opponents' main concern.

The altered wording makes a parent survey seem to back a test-score outcome. Parents were asked about 'academic focus and learning'; test scores come only from the Florida study. The swap tilts the values guide toward the law.

framing_issues.text: which must include hiring a full-time phone monitor
framing_issues.issue: Rewriting 'may include assigning designated school personnel' as a hiring mandate overstates the burden on schools. That tilts toward the enforcement-burden argument against the law (card 5). Line 201 states the rule correctly.

framing_issues.text: 84.7% cited having no way to reach their child in an emergency
framing_issues.issue: Inflating 74.8% to 84.7% in Option B's 'Who pays' overstates the emergency concern on the cost side. Lines 111 and 188 give 74.8%.

framing_issues.text: Our sources give no phone number, email or meeting for lawmakers.
framing_issues.issue: Actionability gap. 'Who decides, and how to reach them' gives a contact only for the governor, whose part is done (and that number is wrong, line 45). It gives none for lawmakers or districts, who make the next decisions. The page is honest about the gap, which is right, but the most useful contacts are missing.
